content.title: About
content.content: Beef with gravy is a dish of boiled or braised beef served with a savory sauce made from meat broth, spices, and sometimes vegetables. It offers a rich flavor, tender meat texture, and a thick, glossy gravy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally it is prepared in colder months because the dish is warming.
Gravy recipes vary worldwide and may include tomato paste, cream, or red wine.
Classic preparation involves slow simmering until the meat is fork‑tender, allowing the flavors to meld.
Beef with gravy is commonly paired with mashed potatoes, rice, or pasta.
Some regions use beef bones to deepen the broth’s flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is one of the best sources of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat supplies B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc from beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Other minerals
items.content: Beef also provides phosphorus and selenium, important for bone health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Large portions can raise cholesterol levels; choosing lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Salt in the gravy
items.content: Gravy often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogens; ensure internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beef hot, sliced into serving pieces. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, boiled rice, pasta, or fresh vegetables. Drizzle the gravy over the meat or use it as a dipping sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese with fruit is a soft, low‑fat (usually 1–2 %) curd cheese that contains pieces of fresh or dried fruit. It has a mild creamy taste, a slight tang, and sweet fruit notes, making it a popular breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cottage cheese is one of the oldest dairy products, known already in ancient Egypt.
Low‑fat versions are widely used in diet plans because they are low in calories but high in protein.
Adding fruit boosts the content of vitamins C and A as well as antioxidants.
Cottage cheese is easily digested and often recommended for children and convalescents.
The product is called cottage cheese in the US and творог in Russia.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Low‑fat cottage cheese provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Fat usually does not exceed 2 %, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: It is a good source of calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamins B2 and B12, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Fruit benefits
items.content: Fruit adds dietary fiber, vitamins C and A, and natural antioxidants.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cottage cheese contains lactose, so people with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared versions can contain added salt; those monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Sugar in fruit
items.content: Dried fruits can raise blood sugar levels; diabetics should prefer fresh fruit without added sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy cottage cheese with fruit as a snack, blend it into smoothies, use it as a filling for pancakes or casseroles, or layer it in dessert parfaits. It also pairs well with honey, nuts, or whole‑grain cereals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2–4 °C. Fresh product remains good for 5–7 days. Freezing may affect texture, so freeze only for long‑term storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Chipotle dip is a creamy sauce made from sour cream and mayonnaise, flavored with smoked chipotle pepper, garlic, lime, and spices. It has a mildly spicy, smoky taste and is perfect for serving with chips, vegetables, tacos, and other Mexican dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chipotle is a smoked, dried, and canned jalapeño pepper that gives the dip its distinctive smoky aroma.
The original recipe was created in the United States in the 1970s as an alternative to traditional salsa.
The sauce is often used as a marinade for chicken, fish, and seafood.
In the US, chipotle dip ranks among the top‑10 most popular fast‑food sauces.
There is a low‑fat version that replaces mayonnaise with yogurt or kefir.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Smoked chipotle peppers contain vitamin C and carotenoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Sour cream and yogurt provide probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Egg‑based mayonnaise supplies a modest amount of vitamin B12, essential for nervous system function.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Sour cream is a good source of calcium, which supports bone health.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat in the dip is monounsaturated, which is considered heart‑friendly.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy base makes the dip calorie‑dense; portion control is advised, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Added salt can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Spicy flavor
items.content: Those sensitive to heat may experience stomach discomfort after consuming the dip.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chipotle dip as a sauce for nachos, tortillas, veggie sticks, grilled chicken, burgers, or as a salad dressing. It can also be mixed into burritos or used as a marinade.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dip refrigerated in a sealed container. Once opened, it stays fresh for 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Classic mixed vegetables (broccoli, carrots, cauliflower, peas) are a ready‑to‑cook frozen blend that has been blanched and sealed in an airtight package. The vegetables retain their natural flavor, bright color, and most of their nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vegetables are harvested at peak season for optimal taste and nutrition.
Steam blanching preserves up to 90 % of B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
The blend can be stored in the freezer for up to 12 months without quality loss.
Uniform piece size allows cooking in 5‑7 minutes in a microwave or steamer.
This mix is widely used in restaurants and cafeterias for quick side dishes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamins
items.content: The mix provides vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and beta‑carotene, important for immunity and vision.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Vegetables have a low energy density, making them a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as lutein and quercetin help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in the vegetables aid normal blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to broccoli or peas.

items.title: Sodium content in seasoned versions
items.content: Certain packages may be salted; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Microbial risk if improperly stored
items.content: Damaged packaging can lead to thawing and create a favorable environment for bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Vegetables can be steamed, microwaved, boiled briefly, or added to soups, stews, and stir‑fries. They work well as a side dish or as a base for vegetable‑rich meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen mix in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, use the product within 3‑4 days and store it in the refrigerator.

lima-beans-and-corn-cooked-fat-added.title: Lima beans and corn, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Lima beans (also called butter beans) and corn cooked together with added fat form a nutritious dish commonly used in stews, soups, and side dishes. Lima beans are large, creamy‑textured, while corn adds sweetness and a crunchy bite. The fat—usually a vegetable oil or butter—enhances flavor and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lima beans are native to South America and were cultivated by the Inca civilization.
Corn was domesticated over 7,000 years ago in Mexico and became a staple crop throughout the Americas.
Combining beans and corn creates a complete protein profile, as the amino acids complement each other.
Traditional Native American recipes often paired these two crops because they were grown side by side.
Adding a small amount of fat increases the bioavailability of corn’s carotenoids.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Lima beans provide about 7 g of protein per 100 g, and corn adds another 3 g, making the dish a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: The bean‑corn combination supplies over 5 g of fiber per serving, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6 and folate
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids amino‑acid metabolism, while folate is essential for DNA synthesis and cell growth.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Lima beans are a decent source of iron (≈2 mg/100 g) and magnesium, which are important for energy production and muscle function.

items.title: Corn antioxidants
items.content: Yellow corn is rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, antioxidants that protect eye health.

items.title: Allergy to legumes or corn
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lima beans or corn.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Because the dish is prepared with added fat, its calorie density is higher; portion control is advised for weight‑management.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking before cooking lowers its level.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause gastrointestinal gas in sensitive people; introduce them gradually.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the beans and corn as a side dish, stir them into soups, chili, salads, or use them in casseroles. Cook the beans until tender, then sauté with a modest amount of oil and add the corn in the last few minutes to keep it crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.

macaroni-or-pasta-salad-made-with-light-.title: Macaroni or Pasta Salad with Light Mayonnaise

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni or pasta salad with light mayonnaise is a cold dish made from cooked pasta, fresh vegetables, and a dressing based on light mayonnaise (3694). It has a mild flavor, a light creamy texture, and works well as a side or a standalone meal for picnics or lunches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light mayonnaise contains less fat and calories than regular mayo, making the salad more diet‑friendly.
Pasta salads are popular in cooler climates as a refreshing summer dish.
Different pasta shapes (spirals, shells, penne) create interesting textural contrasts.
Adding fresh vegetables like cucumber, tomato, and bell pepper boosts the vitamin content.
The salad keeps well in the refrigerator for up to 3 days without losing flavor.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Light mayonnaise reduces the overall fat level, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamin C, potassium, and folate to the dish.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Using whole‑grain pasta increases fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Fresh vegetables raise the water content, helping maintain hydration.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Light mayonnaise often contains eggs; those with an egg allergy should choose an egg‑free version.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared light mayo can be salty; people monitoring sodium intake should control the amount of dressing.

items.title: Bacterial growth
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the salad can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional pasta contains gluten; gluten‑free alternatives are recommended for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta salad chilled, either as a main dish or as a side to meat or fish. It is convenient for lunch boxes, picnics, and barbecues.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. If kept longer than 3 days, check for off‑odors or slimy texture; discard if any signs of spoilage appear.

content.title: About
content.content: Milk is a nutritious white liquid obtained from cows. It contains water, proteins, milk fat, lactose, and minerals. It is sold as whole, skim, and in different fat levels, pasteurized and ultra-pasteurized (UHT). Milk is drunk, added to coffee, tea, porridge, and baked goods, and used to make yogurt, cottage cheese, cheese, and butter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: About 87 percent of milk is water.
Pasteurization, named after Louis Pasteur, heats milk to destroy harmful bacteria.
In homogenization, fat globules are broken up so that cream does not separate.
In many parts of the world, most adults lose some ability to digest lactose.
Milk is made into yogurt, cottage cheese, cheese, cream, butter, and many other products.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium is needed for bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Milk proteins support muscles and help you feel full.

items.title: Contains vitamins B2 and B12
items.content: These vitamins support metabolism and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contains potassium and iodine
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure, and iodine is needed by the thyroid.

items.title: Often fortified with vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: In people with lactose intolerance, lactose causes bloating, cramps, and diarrhea.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Milk allergy can be severe and is different from lactose intolerance.

items.title: Raw milk
items.content: Raw milk may contain dangerous bacteria, so it should be boiled or drunk pasteurized.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Whole milk contains more saturated fat and calories, so with high cholesterol it is better to choose a lower-fat option.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink milk chilled or warm, or add it to coffee, cocoa, tea, porridge, smoothies, pancakes, baked goods, sauces, and desserts. Raw milk must be boiled before drinking. Choose the fat level that suits your diet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store milk in the refrigerator in a closed package and do not leave it at room temperature. After opening, use it within a few days or by the date on the package. Keep unopened UHT cartons in a cool place. Discard milk that smells sour or has curdled.

content.title: About
content.content: Clif Bar is a whole-food energy bar designed for active people and athletes. It contains whole grains, nuts, dried fruit, plant‑based protein, and added vitamins and minerals to support energy and recovery.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Clif Bar was created in 1992 in California as a "cyclist’s energy snack".
Most varieties contain organic rolled oats that provide a slow‑release source of carbohydrates.
The bars are free from artificial flavors, colors, and GMOs.
Clif Bar offers more than 20 flavors, including chocolate, berry, and nut blends.
Each bar is packaged in recyclable material, and the company supports environmental stewardship programs.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Complex carbs from whole grains and fruit deliver a steady flow of glucose during prolonged activity.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Bars provide 9–11 g of protein per serving, helping muscle repair after exercise.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Added B1, B2, B3, and B6 support carbohydrate metabolism and boost endurance.

items.title: Fiber
items.content: Approximately 3 g of fiber per bar promotes healthy digestion and prolonged satiety.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Calcium, iron, and magnesium contribute to bone health and muscle function.

items.title: Nut and soy allergy
items.content: Some varieties contain nuts, peanuts, or soy protein, which may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Bars contain 12–18 g of sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One bar provides about 250 kcal, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed excessively.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Certain flavors include wheat, making them unsuitable for a gluten‑free diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bar is convenient to take to the gym, on a hike, or during travel. Eat it 10–15 minutes before a workout for fuel or right after for recovery. You can also slice the bar and add it to yogurt, oatmeal, or a smoothie.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the package tightly or transfer the bar to an airtight container to maintain its crunchy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Snowpeas are young pea pods harvested before the seeds fully develop. They have a crisp texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and a bright green color. Snowpeas are typically eaten raw in salads, as snacks, or as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snowpeas belong to the legume family and are closely related to garden peas and beans.
Unlike mature peas, the whole pod of snowpeas is edible, skin included.
They are widely used in Asian cuisines, especially Japanese and Chinese dishes.
Snowpeas are rich in antioxidants, notably vitamin C and flavonoids.
They can be grown in temperate climates and are often considered an early harvest crop.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Snowpeas are low in calories, making them a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal blood pressure.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to legumes, including snowpeas.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: As with any fresh produce, snowpeas may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Snowpeas can be eaten raw in salads, added to smoothies, used in spring rolls, or enjoyed as a crunchy snack. They can also be quickly sautéed or blanched to soften the texture while retaining their bright color and crispness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store snowpeas in the refrigerator in an airtight container or bag to keep them fresh for 5‑7 days. For longer storage, freeze the pods in a single layer, then transfer to a freezer‑safe bag.
